name: The Sweet household
head: sweet_alanson

arrival.note: 'Alanson Sweet, 1832' - year precision, the roster's shortest entry. THE COMPILER'S 1832 LIST AGREES AND IS COARSER. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (1895), printed page 89 (claim bk_mose1_001) names this man among those who came through Chicago in 1832 and decided to remain. A YEAR AND NOT A MONTH, from an 1895 compilation, so it corroborates this field and does not move it. THE GRADE CEILING IS THE SOURCE'S AND NOT THIS FIELD'S. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois (1895) is a compiler sixty years after the fact; every claim taken off it is transcription_mediated and none is scan_verified, so nothing drawn from it is graded above `inferred` (the rule T-1322 set for the settlers table, kept here). THE COMPILER GIVES HIM NO STATE, AND THE SILENCE IS PART OF THE READING: the sentence attaches Massachusetts, New York and Vermont to the men before him and closes with a bare "and Alanson Sweet". This card's `origin` therefore stays as the drawn region it was; nothing here replaces it.

origin.note: DRAWN FROM A SURVIVORSHIP SAMPLE. No source says where this household came from. The region is drawn from the birthplaces of the seventy Old Settlers who registered an arrival at or before 1835 — a self-selected roll set down forty-four years later that over-represents the men who stayed and prospered, as the town model's own open questions say. It is the only origin distribution this project holds and this value is drawn from it, not measured.

reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THIS HOUSEHOLD'S OWN RECORDED TRADE, WHICH IS NOT ITS MOTIVE. The head is recorded as tavern keeper, and this names the documented draw that trade answered in this town in this decade. It does not claim to know why these people came. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

last_dated_appearance.note: NO SIGHTING, SO THE LEG IS A SOURCE'S SPAN. The card holds no dated reading of this person at or before the scene date; the date here is the far end of what a cited source COVERS, which the role's own note calls the source's bound and not the man's. Read from `roles[] (source_span)` as `1673/1857`, which reaches 1857-12-31 — a window that covers 1835-07-01 itself, so it pins no last sighting before the day and cannot be read as one. THE FIELD IS THE EVIDENCE UNDER THE VERDICT, not a new claim: nothing here moves the presence off `uncertain`, and T-1159 and T-1172 classify this household by this date instead of reading it out of the prose (T-1144 acceptance 9).

present_on_scene_date.note: PRESENCE ON THE SCENE DATE IS AN ASSUMPTION OF CONTINUITY AND NOT A STATEMENT. Nothing reached follows this household past 1833. It is graded uncertain rather than present because the town's population roughly quadrupled between the roster and the scene date and a great many of the men on it were, in Andreas's own phrase, 'adventurers, comprising moneyed speculators and prospectors, as yet undecided whether to stay at Chicago or go on'.

modelled_family.note: The kin core only. A servant, an apprentice or a journeyman this house may have held is priced by T-1183 and seated by T-1173; a boarder is seated by T-1175. The drawn size is a floor on the house.

ruling.what_happened: STANDS ALONE, AND THAT IS A RULING, NOT A READING. The household model drew this house married at 3 and the order book had no woman left in the wife's cell, and no woman the town already holds fits it. T-2021 ruled that houses like this are given their whole drawn family in a seeded order, while the town the book converges to stays at or under 3,265 people and its under-ten share inside the town model's bracket. The walk stopped at house 157 of 277, and this one came 168, so none of its 2 drawn kin is seated. The head is left as the sources leave him; that is not a claim that he kept no wife.

persons.name: Alanson Sweet

occupation.note: 'Alanson Sweet, 1832' in the roster, with no trade. Andreas supplies it elsewhere: 'In 1833, the first Tremont House, situated then on the northwest corner of Lake and Dearborn streets, was built by Alanson Sweet. It was kept as a saloon and boarding-house by him and a man from Canada, named Darwin.'

dated_bounds.identity_rule: data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json — persons[] person_alanson_sweet, action `enrich` onto this card. The register states its own reason there and this row cites it rather than transcribing it.
dated_bounds.note: AN APPEARANCE IN THE TOWN'S PRINT, AND NOTHING FURTHER. The Chicago Democrat of 1834-12-24 names 'ALANSON SWEET.' in the claim read as chicago_democrat_1834_12_24#c011, so the reading dates an appearance of this person in the town's press and `here_by` is null: a name in print is not a body in the town, and a notice can be signed elsewhere and reprinted here. Under the evidence ladder ratified 2026-09-03 a source EARLIER than the scene date corroborates and dates and never promotes, and a source LATER than it does not promote either. THE IDENTITY IS INFERRED AND THE PAGE IS NOT: the issue is deposited, dated and numbered in data/research/newspapers/corpus.json, and what no source states is that the name the paper prints is the person on this card — the register joins them under its own written note. No grade moves here and the identity is neither reopened nor hardened.

persons.note: Andreas vol. 1, printed p. 132 (scan p. 281), 'an imperfect list of the denizens of the town in the fall of 1833, not before named'. It gives a name, a trade and usually an arrival year, and it is a retrospective of 1884: a YEAR off it is documented, a MONTH is not, and it says nothing whatever about 1835.

resident_research.evidence_for: forenames agree initial for initial: entry 'Alanson Sweet' against resident 'Alanson Sweet'

roles.note: THE BOUND IS THE SOURCE'S, NOT THE MAN'S. This role is carried by the card's 1835 occupation block and is dated by what the cited source or sources are ABOUT, which is why `precision` can be no better than the span they cover. The span reaches 1835, so this role stands in the scene-date view. The printing the trade was read off is not on the card and is fetched by T-1254.

merge_ruling.for_merge: One vowel in the second syllable of a forename on a surname that agrees letter for letter, no middle initial on either side, and the Alanson card is one of the better-evidenced men in the layer: the 1833 tax list (entry 99), the 1834 poll list filed 11 August 1834 (entry 105), the 1835 poll list (entry 78), Kirkland's list of the men of 1832 who stayed, and his own signed caution in the Democrat of 10, 17 and 24 December 1834. Every enumeration of the town inside the window carries exactly ONE Sweet whose forename begins A, and prints it Alanson; the only other Sweet on them is R. M. A householder signing a notice in July 1834 who appears on no roll four weeks later is possible but is the less economical reading.
merge_ruling.against_merge: THE PAGE PRINTS ALONSON, AND IT PRINTS IT AS A SIGNATURE. Read on the scan on 2026-10-09 (the Internet Archive item chicago1835-newspaper-chicago-democrat-1834, Jun1834-Jul1834.pdf, leaf 26 = the issue of 16 July 1834, page 3, column 2, foot): 'Saddles Lost ... July 14, 1834. ALONSON SWEET.' The deposit's 'ALONBON' is the OCR taking the second S for a B; the letter is an S and the vowel before the N is an O, so 'Alon[s]on' is not a mis-read and is not this project's supply. The notice ran a second time on 23 July 1834 (deposit line 3815), set ALONSON again; Alanson's signed caution against a note stands in the issues of 10, 17 and 24 December 1834, set ALANSON every time. SEARCHED, the whole deposit (73 Democrat issues, the Chicago American of June to August 1835) and the reading index, for both spellings: ALONSON twice, both insertions of the one July notice; ALANSON three times, all in that December 1834 caution; 'A. SWEET' on the to-let and warehouse advertisements of December 1833 to August 1834 and the town-meeting committee of 17 June 1835, which an initial cannot decide. NO single printing — one issue, one roll, one directory entry — sets both spellings for one man, so the printer is never caught varying, which is C10's load-bearing clause. Each spelling is steady across its own repeated insertions, but a notice kept standing in type is one setting printed twice and not two witnesses, so that steadiness distinguishes nothing either way. C12 cannot fire: a poll list bounds who VOTED, not who lived here, and no non-name fact puts the July subscriber on it. D8. THIS IS NOT A CLAIM THAT THE TOWN HELD TWO MEN OF THE NAME; it is the ruling that nothing reached folds them, and that the initial A therefore still has two full forenames to fit (R2), so 'A. Sweet' stays on a card of its own.

basis.note: Drawn from the 1840 Chicago schedule's column 'free white males 40 under 50', one of its male bands, conditioned on `named_on_a_roll_15_and_over` because the person is named in their own right on any other roll this layer was minted from - a letter list, a subscription, a court docket, a trade notice - or carries a role, a trade, a marriage or a parenthood.

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('sweet_alanson:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

research_note: THE MAN WHO BUILT THE TREMONT AND SOLD IT. He put the house up in 1833, kept it as a saloon and boarding house with a Canadian named Darwin, and the Couch brothers then bought it - which is why Ira Couch and not Alanson Sweet is linked to tremont_house_1 in this parcel. What Sweet was doing on 1 July 1835 is not stated anywhere reached, and the occupation recorded here is the one he is documented in rather than the one he then had. HIS PARTNER DARWIN IS A DOCUMENTED RESIDENT WITH A SURNAME, A TRADE AND AN ORIGIN ('a man from Canada') and is not written as a household, because a boarding-house partner in 1833 whose given name is unknown and who is never mentioned again is exactly the kind of entry that would inflate the count without adding evidence. He is recorded in data/residents/index.json among the people researched and not written.
